title: Mastering Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO): From Pathophysiology to Management
summary: CRVO represents a spectrum of retinal venous outflow obstruction ranging from perfusion-stable to ischemic variants. This guide delineates the diagnostic workup, systemic associations by age, and the precise indications for anti-VEGF therapy versus panretinal photocoagulation (PRP).

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: CRVO is characterized by obstruction of the central retinal vein at or posterior to the lamina cribrosa. Pathophysiology follows 'Hayreh’s criteria' involving venous stasis, turbulent flow, and secondary endothelial damage. The resulting hydrostatic pressure elevation leads to intraretinal hemorrhage, macular edema, and ischemia.

rows: Factor V Leiden, Protein C/S deficiency

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup (The 10-Point Plan)
content: 1. Best Corrected Visual Acuity (BCVA)
2. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (Iris neovascularization search)
3. Gonioscopy (Mandatory before treatment)
4. Fundus examination (7-field photography)
5. OCT (Macular thickness/Cystoid changes)
6. Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) - Gold Standard
7. IOP measurement
8. Blood Pressure check
9. CBC/ESR/CRP/HbA1c/Lipid profile
10. Thrombophilia screen (If <50y)

sections.title: When to perform PRP?
content: Perform panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) immediately upon detection of NVI (Neovascularization of the Iris) or NVA (Neovascularization of the Angle).
Prophylactic PRP is NOT indicated in non-ischemic CRVO, as conversion rates to ischemic CRVO are variable.
Follow up every 4 weeks for the first 6 months to detect the '100-day glaucoma' window.

sections.title: Role of Anti-VEGF Therapy
content: Indicated primarily for macular edema (ME) secondary to CRVO (BRAVO/CRUISE trials).
Anti-VEGF agents (Ranibizumab, Aflibercept, Bevacizumab) reduce VEGF-induced vascular permeability.
Pro-re-nata (PRN) or Treat-and-Extend (T&E) dosing is standard until BCVA stabilizes and OCT shows resolution of cystic edema.
Anti-VEGFs do not 'cure' the ischemia; they suppress the secondary effects of ischemia (edema and neovascularization).

content.explanation: C-Carotid artery stenosis (Ocular Ischemic Syndrome), R-Retinopathy (Diabetic), V-Venous stasis (Hemi-CRVO), O-Others (Hyperviscosity), D-Disc edema, I-Inflammation (Vasculitis), F-Fundus (Hemorrhagic glaucoma)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Landmarks
content: The '100-day glaucoma' (Neovascular glaucoma) typically appears within 3-4 months of onset.
CRUISE trial: Showed superiority of Ranibizumab vs Sham in improving BCVA.
Ischemic definition: >10 disc area of non-perfusion on FFA.
Always evaluate for POAG in the contralateral eye.
